## Sampling sites

[valentin.moser@wsl.ch](mailto:valentin.moser@wsl.ch)

We joined an ongoing experiment which sampled 8 sites with active beaver dams in the Swiss low-lands (see FIGURE X \- map). The sampling period with the active samplers was from July 5th to July 12th 2024 and the passive samplers were deployed on July 14th and collected on July 31st 2024\. For the active samplers, the sites were sampled consecutively, beginning with Dübendorf (the site closest to Zürich), followed by Le Talent (the most western site in the succession), and then proceeding from west to east. For the passive samplers, all samplers were installed and collected with 24 hours of each other.

## Sampling

We compared the following six active samplers: (1) Kärcher impinger (REF Jakob), (2) The Coriolis µ,  
(3) the Burkhard Cyclon sampler (4) an Electrostatic precipitator, (5) a HEPA sampler (ref Lynngaard and Bohman) (6) The Sass 3100 dry filter sampler and at three occasions a Drone mounted with two grease covered plates under two propellers, acting as impingers.

We also compared two passive samplers: The filter sampler from WSL [markus.schlegel@wsl.ch](mailto:markus.schlegel@wsl.ch) and a Modified Wilson and Cook trap (Ref Johson 2017 master thesis)  
   
The active samplers were operated in parallel, next to each other, close to the shore of the pool created by the beaver dams. 

FIGURE X

![][image2]  
From left to right: Coriolis µ with long-term sampling option, Kärcher impinger, Electrostatic precipitator, HEPA sampler, SASS 3200, Burkhard cyclon sampler. 

 A first set of samples was taken for a duration of 30 min, after which the samples were collected and the sampler were restarted for a second sampling period of 5h. The samplers were not cleaned between the short and long sampling on the same day. We operated the samplers and collected the samples as follows:  
 

### Kärcher

The Kärcher was operated as previously described (REF). Four water filters were sterilized in the laboratory with 10% bleach solution and rinsed thoroughly with Milli-Q water. Subsequently, the air opening was sealed with parafilm to ensure sterility during storage and transportation in the field. To minimize the collection of whole insects, the Kärcher was equipped with a custom-built plastic plate that held a metal paper basket. In the field, the paper basket was sterilized with bleach and rinsed with Milli-Q water, and a pre-sterilized insect net (REF) was fitted around the paper basket and secured at the base using a clamping belt. The insect nets were sterilized with bleach, rinsed with Milli-Q water, and transported to the field inside 1 L zip-lock bags to maintain sterility.

As sampling liquid, we used 2L of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) buffer at a concentration of 1X. The buffer was sterilized under ultraviolet (UV) light inside a laboratory cleanroom. The liquid was subjected to UV irradiation for a minimum of 45 minutes. The sterilized buffer was transported into the field in pre-sterilized 1L plastic bottles.   
   
During the 5 h Sampling period we monitored the evaporation of the sampling liquid hourly and replaced evaporated liquid with UV’ed milli-Q water to not alter the buffer concentration. The water was sampled by pouring the liquid back into the Bottles which previously contained the sampling buffer and then filtering the liquid onto 0.22 µm Sterivex filters \[REF\] using a 50 ml syringe. The samples were preserved with 2 ml Longmire buffer (without SDS), closed with luer stoppers at both ends (or parafilm in case of a luer fitter outlet), placed into a 50 ml falcon tube and stored at room temperature. The Longmire buffer was sterile-filtered, UV’ed for 45 min and pre-filled into 3 ml Syringes at a sterile bench. We closed the syringes with luer stoppers and transported them into individual zip-log bags together with a sterile 50 ml syringe (bleach cleaned and rinsed with milli-Q).  
   
The Kärcher was placed onto a camping table (height \~1m ? ) and powered by a generator.  
   
The sampler was sterilzed at the start of each sampling day by wiping air inlet, the paper basket holder and the paper basket with bleach and milli-q. Four water filters and insect nets were pre-sterilised in the lab and transpozted to the filed. After 4 days, we re-sterilzed the water filters and insect nets by submerging and washing them in 20 L of bleach (transported in a water-tight box) and drying off the bleach with paper towels and subsequently rinsing them with large amount of milli-q water and csealing the air inlet with parafilm / storing the clean nets in fresh zip-log bags.

The Kärcher has a nominal flow rate of 3000 L / min, corresponding to a sampled air volume of 90 '000 L for 30 min and 900' 000 L for 5 hours.

### Coriolis 

The Coriolis was operated at a sampling rate of 300 L per minute. The samples were collected into a sterile sampling cone (individually packed, custom produced for the Coriolis by Bertin Instruments) and filled with 15 ml PBS as sampling liquid. We operated the Coriolis with the long-term sampling option, consisting of a peristaltic pump which continuously replaced the evaporated sampling liquid  with sterile filtered and UV’ed Milli-Q water at a fixed rate. The replacement rate was between 0.7 – 0.9 ml per minute and adjusted manually to daily conditions (temperature, humidity and sampling in shade or sun-shine). We paused the sampling periodically to check the remaining liquid and adjusted the replacement rate if necessary.  
   
We filtered the Coriolis sample onto a 0.22 µm Polycarbonate filter paper (25 mm diameter ?) pre-mounted in a bleached and UV-sterilzed filter holder unit transported into the field in individual zip-log bags. The filter was then immediately placed into a 2 ml tube with sterile syringes (bleachen and rinsed with milli-q in the field immediately before sampling) and preserved with \~1.5 ml Longmire buffer solution (without SDS).   
   
The Coriolis was placed onto a camping table (height \~1m ? ) and powered by a generator.  
   
The sampler was sterilized by washing the sampling head with bleach and rinsing it with milli-q at the start and at the end of each day. In addition, we ran the sampler with a rinsed cone filled with UV’ed milli-Q water for 2 X 1 min at the start of each day to flush the sampler with local air.

At a flow rate of 300 L / min corresponds to a sampled air volume of 9 '000 L for 30 min and 90 ‘000 L for 5 hours.

### HEPA 

The HEPA Sampler was built following the instructions provided by (REF Lynggaard et al 2022\) with the modification that the ring holding the filter in place was screwed onto the filter holder instead of fitting over it. As filter material we purchased a commercial HEPA filter, removed the filter fleece from its frame, stretched it out and cut out round 90 mm filters out of it. The filters were then sterilized with UV light for 45 min on each side and transported in a sterilized zip-log bag. The fan was powered with the generator using a 240V transformer [stefano.mintchev@usys.ethz.ch](mailto:stefano.mintchev@usys.ethz.ch) but could easily be powered by a battery instead.  
   
We mounted the sampler on a camera tripod with rubber bands. The filter was not protected with a metal screen so we cannot exclude that some insects might have interacted with the filter directly but no insect got stuck onto the filter.  
   
After sampling, we cut out the exposed area of the filter with a bleach-sterilized carpet-knife (?) handling the filter with sterilized tweezers. The filter was placed in a 7 ml screw-cap tube and preserved with 3 ml Longmire buffer. We used the syringe to make sure that the whole filter was soaked into the preservation buffer by pushing the buffer into the filter and sucking it through the filter repeatedly.  
   
The HEPA sampler was sterilzed by whipping the surface in contact with the filter with bleach and rinsing it with milli-Q water.

We measured the flow rate of the HEPA sampler using a thermal anemometer (testo 405i), measuring an air speed of XX m/s. Given the are of the exposed filter, this corresponds to a flow rate of \~60 L /min ([stefano.mintchev@usys.ethz.ch](mailto:stefano.mintchev@usys.ethz.ch) we might need to re-measure). 

This corresponds to a sampled air volume of 1800 L for 30 min and 18 000 L for 5 hours. 

### Electrostatic Precipitator 

[stefano.mintchev@usys.ethz.ch](mailto:stefano.mintchev@usys.ethz.ch) for description. 

The electrostatic precipitator was constructed based on the prototype described by Priyamvada et al. (2021), designed for particle collection in the size range of 0.01-10 µm. It consists of an air ionizer followed by two parallel stainless steel electrodes charged at 5 kV to generate an electric field, and an electric fan. The fan pulls air through the positive ionizer, inducing a charge on the airborne particles. These charged particles are then attracted to the negative electrode by the electric field, where they deposit.

We mounted the sampler onto a camera tripod (height?), where it was fixed with a 3D printed foot. For sampling, we unmounted the sampler, released the nylon silicon screws holding the sampling plates in place and placed both the plates with the sampling side up on the sampling station. We swabbed the plates with sterile swabs (REF) soaked in Longmire buffer, carefully swabbing the whole plate and rotating the swab while sampling to take up all potential particles (there was no perceptible deposition using the bare eye). We then placed both swab heads together into a 2 ml screw cap tube, broke off the tails and added enough sampling buffer to the tube to cover both swab-tips (\~1.5 ml).  
   
The sampler was sterilized by wiping the metal plates with bleach and rinsing them with milli-Q water. In addition, at each site and before the first sampling of the day, the sampler was flushed with air for approximately 10 min, with the ventilator put on the highest level but the ionizer turned off and no tension on the sampling plates.  
   
The Sampler was operated by the generator in combination with a 12V transformer but could easily be operated by a battery.

The nominal air flow of the electrostatic precipitators was \~10 L /min across the two plates, which corresponds to the recommended flow rate for optimal sampling efficiency (REF). This corresponds to a sampled air volume of 300 L for 30 min and 3000 L for 5 hours.

### Drone

Hovering UAVs, such as quadcopters, can be regarded as "flying hoovers" because their propellers pull in and accelerate large volumes of air to generate the thrust required for flight. During a 30-minute flight, a 250-gram quadcopter can accelerate up to 3 × 10^5 liters of air, substantially exceeding the air collection capacity of filter-based air samplers. We tested the feasibility of collecting airborne eDNA with a drone by integrating two impactors beneath the front propellers of a DJI Mavic Mini. The impactors intercept the particles accelerated by the propellers with a 1 × 4 cm flat adhesive surface coated with silicone grease (ADD reference).

Before each flight, the impactors were sterilised by wiping them with bleach and rinsing them with Milli-Q water. A thin layer of sterilised silicone grease was applied to the surface of the impactor and evenly spread using a sterilised metal spatula. The two impactors were mounted under the front propellers and secured with rubber bands to the drone structure. The drone was manually flown back and forth above the beaver dams at an altitude between 5 and 10 metres for 15 minutes. After landing, we swabbed each impactor with sterile swabs, carefully removing the silicone from the entire plate. Both swab heads were then placed together into a 2 ml screw cap tube, with the tails broken off, and enough sampling buffer was added to cover both swab tips (\~1.5 ml).

### MWAC trap

We built the Modified Wilson and Cook samplers following instruction from Dr. Mendez and Mariano Javier  
(Instituto de Ciencias de la Tierra y Ambientales de La pampa). 

The MWAC sampler was developed by Wilson and Cook (1980) and consists of a closed polyethylene bottle, an inlet tube, and an outlet tube. The bottle serves as the settling chamber and the two plastic tubes pass air through the cap into the bottle and then out again. Due to the larger volume of the bottle relative to the inlet diameter, dust particles entering the bottle experience a flow deceleration and are deposited inside the bottle. The air then discharges from the bottle via the outlet tube. The MWAC sampler is commonly used in soil erosion studies and was validated as airborne eDNA sampler by REF Jonsson et al 2017\. The efficiency of the MWAC sampler depends on wind speed and particle size and has been found to reach from 0 \- 20% with higher efficiency for larger particles with the dependency of wind speed being inconclusive (likely because of particle resuspension) (REF Mendez et al., 2016). 

Our MWAC trap design used 1L XXX bottles with specific dimensions (XXX). The inlet and outlet tubes had specified inner and outer diameters (XX) and were constructed from flexible metal conduit with plastic inner and outer layers. Three traps were attached to a rotating pole, with the tubes parallel to the ground. Wind sails were mounted on the poles to ensure the inlet tubes faced the incoming wind. The bottles were tilted at a 45° angle. Since the goal was to collect airborne eDNA, not quantify dust, we added 100 ml of sampling buffer to each bottle (with the tubes not reaching the liquid). The buffer did not fully evaporate after two weeks of sampling, but the remaining volume varied based on the sampler location.

When collecting samples, the inlet and outlet were sealed with parafilm, and the bottles were transported to the lab. The liquid from the three bottles attached to each pole was combined and filtered through a 0.22 µm polycarbonate filter paper (diameter 25 mm). The filter was transferred to a 2 ml tube using sterile syringes, and the sample was preserved with \~1.5 ml Longmire buffer solution (without SDS).

As a negative control, two sample bottles that remained unsampled were filled with 100 ml of buffer solution, shaken, and filtered following the same procedure used for the field samples.

### Passive filter traps (WSL) 

[markus.schlegel@wsl.ch](mailto:markus.schlegel@wsl.ch)  
 Deposition was collected on glass fiber filters following the method evaluated by Schlegel et al. (2024). Filters of 81 mm diameter (Whatman No. 1820-6537) were secured to the bottom side of sterile Petri dishes of 94 mm diameter (Greiner Bio-One, St. Gallen, Switzerland) inside a laminar flow cabinet. Attachment was achieved by applying three small drops of water-resistant glue (Cementit Universal, Kolma AG, Switzerland) along the edge. To prevent microbial growth, filters were further treated with 2 ml of 4X TE buffer (40 mM Tris HCl and 4 mM EDTA, pH 8.0) in accordance with previous studies (Schweigkofler et al. 2004; Redondo et al. 2020). After drying for 1:15 h, they were exposed to UV light for 30 minutes. The filters were then covered with the lids of the Petri dishes to protect the surface during transport and placed in clean zip-lock bags, which were further irradiated with UV on both sides and stored at room temperature until use.  
At the start of the two-week sampling period, the Petri dishes were mounted 5 cm below an octagonal roof (20 cm diameter), and the lids were removed. After exposure, the filters were covered with fresh lids and stored in clean zip-lock bags. For further processing, filters were carefully removed by using …, cutting around the glue drops and stored in …. DNA extraction was performed from one half? of the filter...

### Insect cover

   
The air inlet of the Coriolis, the SASS and the Burkhard sampler were covered with a brass insect screen \~1 mm mesh size, that was replaced daily and sterilised with bleach and rinsed with milli-Q before mounting around the inlet. The inlet of the Kärcher was mounted with an insect net. We did this to prevent sucking in full insects or large chunks of plant material which risks dominating the DNA pool and drowning out the trace DNA from other species. However, very small insects could pass through the screens and were sucked into the samples at multiple occasions, especially for the Coriolis and the Kärcher that sampled into liquid at high flow rates. The SASS sampler also sucked in small insects (thrips?) occasionally but to a lesser extent. If possible we remove whole insects and any other fragments visible with the bare eye before collecting the samples.   
 

### Field negative controls

   
We collected field negative controls at two occasions on day 4 and day 8 of the sampling campaign. Negative controls were taken by mounting the samplers as normally but collecting the samples without starting the samplers before the first sampling of the day. For the Kärcher, we filled the water filter with the sampling liquid making sure that the buffer got in contact with all parts of the water filter and subsequently sampled 100ml with two falcon tubes. For the Coriolis, we filled the sampling cone with 15ml PBS and added 5 ml of the milli-q water using the peristaltic pump. The combined sample was taken as negative control. For the field negative controls, all samples were processed and stored as the normal samples.

## Bioinformatics

Current analysis. Please adapt and complement accordingly. 

#### Demultiplexing: see Demultiplexing\_by\_Primer.Rmd

####  

Total reads: 202.5 Million sequence (after phiX removal)

**bbduk**  
I use bbduk to filter reads containing N's and remaining PhiX, with maxns \= 0

Reads with N’s: 14%  
Phix  remaining: 0.8%

**Cutadapt**  
I use cutadapt version 4.8 for paired-end read trimming and demultiplexing by primer sequence. Parameters include: 12 bp minimum overlap at the read start for the primer. The reverse complement of the primer at the read end is trimmed if found but not mandatory (as it depends on the amplicon length). Up to 10% mismatch rate is allowed (default). Reads without adaptors are discarded. All primers of the primer mix are provided for fungi.

\>98% of reads which passed the bbduk filter matched one of the primers in any non-control sample. 

#### ASV inference see \*\_Seq\_analysis.Rmd

DADA2 version 1.32.0

In general the read quality was very high and over the full length of the reads. 

Trimming parameters were as follows: 

**Vertebrates**: no trimming, maxEE=c(1,1). The expected fragment length was 204 bps, the ends of the reads have already been trimmed down from 300 bps in cutadapt. 

**Arthropods:** I trimmed down the reverse reads to 160 bps. maxEE=c(1,1). The expected fragment length was 350 bps

**Plants:** the merged fragments are 471 bp long. I trim reverse reads to 230 bps (80 bs min overlap). maxEE=c(1,2)

**Fungi:** the largest peak of the merged fragments was 387 bps long. I trim the reverse reads to 200 bps.  maxEE=c(1,1)

**Bacteria:** the merged fragments are 253 bp long. We trim reverse read to 160 bps. maxEE=c(1,1)

The next steps are expected error filtering, denoising and merging and chimaera removal (all with default parameters) 

**Clustering**

For all taxa but vertebrates, I used swarm-3.1.0 (REF Mahé et al) for a first clustering of the OTU sequences. With d \= 1 and fastidious option. Swarm is a single-linkage clustering algorithm with variable cut-off. However, with d \= 1, the vast majority of clusters have a similarity of \>99%, making overclustering at this step very unlikely. 

**Taxonomy**

For all taxa but vertebrates I used vsearch v2.17.0 \--sintax (an adaptation of the utax algorith, implementing the rdp classifier) with the a cutoff of 0.1 (keeping all best taxonomic guesses, we filter later) with the following reference datasets: 

**Bacteria:** 

I use the rdp trainset19\_072023  
downloaded from \[here\](https://mothur.org/wiki/rdp\_reference\_files/)  
accessed on "2024-05-23"

I formatted the sequences names for SINTAX. The database does not contain species level assignments, the lowest level is genus level. 

**Fungi:**

https://unite.ut.ee/repository.php

Abarenkov, Kessy; Zirk, Allan; Piirmann, Timo; Pöhönen, Raivo; Ivanov, Filipp; Nilsson, R. Henrik; Kõljalg, Urmas (2022): UNITE general FASTA release for eukaryotes 2\. Version 16.10.2022. UNITE Community. https://doi.org/10.15156/BIO/2483914

Includes global and 3% distance singletons. 

I harmonised the taxonomy against the Gbif backbone and formatted the refDB for Sintax

**Plants:**

I download the PLANiTS database from \[here\](https://github.com/apallavicini/PLANiTS/blob/master/PLANiTS\_29-03-2020.zip) 

The article describing the database can be found \[here\]([https://academic.oup.com/database/article/doi/10.1093/database/baz155/5722079](https://academic.oup.com/database/article/doi/10.1093/database/baz155/5722079))

**Arthropods:**

Leray M, Knowlton N, Machida RJ.. MIDORI2: A collection of quality controlled, preformatted, and regularly updated reference databases for taxonomic assignment of eukaryotic mitochondrial sequences. Environmental DNA n/a. (doi:10.1002/edn3.303)

[https://www.reference-midori.info/download/Databases/GenBank259\_2023-12-17/SINTAX\_sp/uniq/MIDORI2\_UNIQ\_NUC\_SP\_GB259\_CO1\_SINTAX.fasta.gz](https://www.reference-midori.info/download/Databases/GenBank259_2023-12-17/SINTAX_sp/uniq/MIDORI2_UNIQ_NUC_SP_GB259_CO1_SINTAX.fasta.gz)

**Vertebrates:**  
I blast the ASV sequences with Standard Nucleotide BLAST on NCBI against the nt database (full nucleotide collection) Highly similar sequences (megablast)

**Taxonomic clustering**

(all but vertebrates). 

I harmonise the taxonomy against the gbif backbone. Then I apply a confidence threshold of 80% bootstrap confidence, setting all taxonomic levels with lower confidence to NA. 

I cluster sequences assigned to same species or genus (if species is NA)

I use phyloseq \[REF\] to merge ASVs with the same taxonomic assignment at species level, or genus level if a species level assignment is missing. If both are missing we do not merge the sequences. 

Vertebrates: I manually curated the taxonomy based on the best blast hits (will expand description here)

If you would like to use a different analysis pipeline, modify it, or use a different reference database please adapt and complement accordingly. 

The taxonomy would need to be double-checked.

Question: How does the community composition differ between Samplers and Sites? 

This NMDS plot is based on Bray-Curtis dissimilarity between samples (rarefied data, presence / absence). 

Problems & to-do: Bray Curtis is calculated as the fraction of shared species over all species. This means that difference in richness drives difference in community composition which leads to a strong sampler effect. 

We should try to disentangle the two effects, i.e. difference in Samplers after accounting for Site and difference in Site after accounting for Sampler (and duration). 

Statistically this is possible (marginal effects), for plotting the richness differences drive the pattern.  

![][image8]

![][image9]

### Community correlation

Question: Does the difference / similarity in community composition across sites correlate between different samplers? 

This is a correlation matrix between the differences in community composition across sites. There are 8 sites, so 28 site combinations. For each sampler X duration I extract the 28 similarity values for the site combinations and correlate them with the dissimilarities obtained from other Samplers. Significance is not yet accounted for.  Not all correlations are meaningful, it might be better to only present a subset.

## Plants

### Comparison with species list

Here I compare at genus level. At species level the taxonomy needs to be double-checked and manually curated as right now we assign against a global reference database. 

Across all sites, the manual survey detected 128 genera of vascular plants. Across both markers, we detect 102 / 128 genera. 

![][image38]  
We detect 19 genera which are not part of the Swiss flora (According to the species list of vascular plants for Switzerland). Most species seem to be ornamental plants and/or food items (cashews, banana). → should probably be excluded from other analysis

### Comparison with species list

We have reference data collected on site, but I haven’t seen them yet. We can also compare for certain case-studies, e.g. Dragonflies were present and abundant at many sites but we have a single detection of a single species in one sample. Even the Kärcher sample, where dragonflies were sitting on the sampler during sampling, did not detect them. Need also to check Primer bias. 

### Primer eval

We had designed new primers to avoid co-amplification of Fungi. 

![][image51]

![][image52]

The co-amplification of fungi was significantly smaller than what I have seen in other dataset. However, these primers co-amplify plant sequences. There is also a large fraction of reads that cannot be assigned, blasting the most sequences gives no insightful results. 

Nevertheless, 30% target amplification is more than what I have previously seen with other primers, and the remaining depth was sufficient.
